clinicalPearls: Complete absence of functional and antigenic fibrinogen due to biallelic loss-of-function mutations in FGA, FGB or FGG, inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern.
Umbilical cord stump bleeding in a neonate is a classic and often first presentation.
All clot-based coagulation tests are markedly prolonged because fibrin is the common endpoint — prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, thrombin time and reptilase time.
Paradoxical arterial and venous thrombosis can occur despite the bleeding tendency, both spontaneously and after fibrinogen replacement.
Spontaneous splenic rupture and intracranial haemorrhage are feared, potentially fatal complications.
Recurrent early pregnancy loss and placental abruption occur because fibrinogen is essential for maintaining placental integrity.
Fibrinogen concentrate is the treatment of choice, used therapeutically and prophylactically around surgery, trauma and pregnancy.
Distinguish from dysfibrinogenaemia (dysfunctional protein, near-normal antigen) and hypofibrinogenaemia (reduced quantity).
reference.pathophysiology: Fibrinogen is a large hexameric glycoprotein composed of paired Aa, Bb and g chains, synthesised in the liver and encoded by the clustered FGA, FGB and FGG genes on chromosome 4. In congenital afibrinogenaemia, biallelic loss-of-function mutations abolish production or secretion of intact fibrinogen, leaving plasma essentially devoid of the protein. Because fibrinogen is the terminal substrate of the coagulation cascade — cleaved by thrombin into fibrin monomers that polymerise into the clot scaffold and are then cross-linked by factor XIII — its absence prevents stable clot formation and produces a lifelong bleeding tendency. Fibrinogen is also the principal ligand bridging activated platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors, so primary haemostasis is simultaneously impaired despite a normal platelet count. The paradoxical thrombotic risk is thought to arise partly because fibrinogen normally binds and sequesters thrombin (its antithrombin-I activity); without this buffering, unbound thrombin persists, and abnormal or infused fibrin can precipitate clotting.
additionalDifferentials: Disseminated intravascular coagulation causing acquired hypofibrinogenaemia
Severe liver disease with reduced fibrinogen synthesis
Factor XIII deficiency (normal routine clotting tests but poor clot stability and umbilical bleeding)
Combined deficiency of factor V and factor VIII and other severe neonatal factor deficiencies
Vitamin K deficiency bleeding of the newborn
additionalInvestigations: Functional (Clauss) fibrinogen assay alongside an immunological antigenic fibrinogen level
Prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time
Molecular genetic testing of FGA, FGB and FGG
Family studies with parental fibrinogen levels
Cranial imaging when intracranial haemorrhage is suspected
redFlags: Features of intracranial haemorrhage such as altered consciousness, focal neurological deficit or a bulging fontanelle in an infant
Sudden severe abdominal pain with circulatory collapse suggesting spontaneous splenic rupture
Uncontrolled bleeding after minor trauma, surgery or venepuncture
First-trimester bleeding or recurrent pregnancy loss
reference.prognosis: With fibrinogen replacement and specialist haemostatic care the outlook is generally good, but intracranial haemorrhage remains a leading cause of death and both bleeding and thrombotic complications require lifelong, individualised management.
pitfalls: Regarding the disorder as purely a bleeding diathesis and overlooking the genuine thrombotic risk, including after replacement therapy.
Forgetting that platelet aggregation is impaired despite a normal platelet count.
Attributing an unmeasurable fibrinogen solely to disseminated intravascular coagulation or liver disease without considering a congenital cause.
Failing to provide prophylactic replacement around surgery, trauma and throughout pregnancy.
Confusing afibrinogenaemia with dysfibrinogenaemia, in which antigen is near normal but function is reduced.
management: Replace fibrinogen with fibrinogen concentrate (or cryoprecipitate) to treat active bleeding and as prophylaxis for surgery and high-risk situations
Give prophylactic fibrinogen replacement throughout pregnancy to reduce miscarriage and placental abruption
Use antifibrinolytic agents such as tranexamic acid as adjuncts for mucosal bleeding, and avoid antiplatelet drugs and NSAIDs
Balance replacement carefully and consider thromboprophylaxis because of the paradoxical arterial and venous thrombosis risk
Escalate urgently with fibrinogen replacement and imaging for suspected intracranial haemorrhage or splenic rupture
Deliver care through a specialist haemostasis or haemophilia centre with an individualised treatment plan
Offer genetic counselling given autosomal recessive FGA, FGB or FGG inheritance
